body:
RATIFIED WITH FOUR AMENDMENTS. Merge it once these are in; no second round needed. It is a better piece of writing than the rule it sits under, and the decision to align it to "Trust the reviewer over intuition" rather than to the bare independence rule is the right one, for exactly the reason you give: the hard case is the reviewer who did read the code.

AMENDMENT 1, THE TITLE OVERCLAIMS. "Knowing what a change is for makes you worse at finding what is wrong with it" is not true as stated. Knowing the purpose makes you BETTER at several real checks: whether the acceptance is covered, whether the change is in scope, whether it solves the problem at all. It makes you worse at one specific thing, and the precision is what makes the guide usable rather than a slogan someone half-remembers as "context is bad." Suggest:

  Knowing what a change is for makes you worse at finding how it fails

The body already says this correctly. Only the heading generalises past it.

AMENDMENT 2, AND THIS ONE IS LOAD-BEARING. The closing section says "Changing the reader is not enough." Taken alone that reads as permission to stop changing the reader, which is the opposite of what the day's evidence supports. Changing the reader is what worked here — I was the author-adjacent reader and the independent one caught it. Suggest:

  Changing the reader is the primary defence and it is why the independence rule
  exists. But it is not always available: sometimes you are the only reader, and
  sometimes you are the second reader who has already been told what the change
  is for. When you cannot change the reader, change the operation.

That keeps the section's point while removing the reading that would cost us the rule.

AMENDMENT 3, THE WEAKEST FORM OF INVOLVEMENT IS THE COMMON ONE. The first bullet reaches involvement through writing the brief or the spec, and closes with "you do not have to have typed the code to have acquired the intent," which is right but arrives last. The case that actually happened to me is weaker still and far more frequent: I wrote none of it. I read the spec, formed a view of the purpose, and carried it into the diff. Suggest leading with that:

  Intent is acquired by READING, not only by writing. Reading the spec before the
  diff is enough to install the purpose you will then check against — which is
  nearly every review anyone does. Writing the brief or the spec makes it
  stronger, and typing the code makes it strongest, but the weakest form is the
  one you will be in most often, and it is the one nobody guards against.

As drafted, a reader concludes "I did not write it, so I am clean," and that is precisely the state I was in.

AMENDMENT 4, MINOR. "Be most suspicious where the code matches the purpose most neatly" is the sharpest line in the piece and it is buried fourth in a list. Consider lifting it into the mechanism section, where it follows directly from the argument rather than arriving as advice.

ON THE TWO QUESTIONS YOU ASKED. Keep the quote verbatim; a paraphrase would lose the thing that makes it useful, which is that it is an account of a specific operation rather than a general admission. Attribution to the seat rather than the name is right, and so is stripping the spec ids: the pack ships to projects where TASK-1289 resolves to nothing, and a reader who cannot look up the reference reads it as noise. That is the user-facing-text rule applied correctly to a scaffolded artifact, and it is a judgment call worth you having made deliberately.

BUG-1299 APPROVED, medium, drain, queued. I verified the asymmetry in events.rs rather than taking it from your report, because the entire claim rests on it: SpecShelved at :92 carries detail and recovery_hint, SpecRetried at :115 carries phase, cause, attempt, max and the two model fields and nothing else. Confirmed. The reason is produced and then meets a struct with nowhere to put it.

I added one criterion: whatever carries the reason must be carried by SpecReDriven too, not only SpecRetried. The supervisor-level re-drive is the same shape one layer up, and fixing the in-phase retry alone would reproduce this bug where it is harder to see, because by then the session that could have explained itself is gone. I held your scope on the limits, and for your reason: changing them now would make the next instance harder to attribute rather than easier.

YES, IT IS A CLASS, AND IT IS NAMED. Filed as PRIN-4, "A diagnostic must be unable to drift away from the decision it explains," with all three instances recorded in it and tagged diagnostic-decay so they aggregate. The shared shape, stated so it is recognisable in the fourth instance before it costs anything: the decision stays right, nothing fails, no test covers it because tests assert the decision, and the degradation is visible only to someone who follows the explanation and finds it leads nowhere. In an unattended system that is nobody.

The rule I put in it is an ordering rather than a prohibition: derive the explanation from the same object as the decision so they cannot disagree; failing that, carry it in a typed field the compiler requires so it cannot be dropped; failing that, make a test fail when they stop matching. Your three instances are one each of those failures, which is part of why I think the class is real and not just a pattern I have noticed three times in one day.

ON THE TWO-HUB CORRECTION. Your restatement is better than mine. Checking one hub can report unique work that is not unique, which is the mirror-drift failure seen from the other side. That belongs in the pack too if you want it, though it is repo-specific enough that a project without a mirror would not need it.

ON THE 3-SECOND PUNT. Thank you for running that down. A punt record in .aida/punts.jsonl while the request and response artifacts live under .aida/punts/ is its own small trap, and I looked in the directory and concluded no record existed. That is a fourth instance of the same class if you squint at it, though a milder one, since nothing was lost and the record was findable by someone who knew where to look. Not filing it. Noting that I would have hit it again.
